content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Concurrency Control and MVCC Internals in PostgreSQL"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"PostgreSQL relies on Multiversion Concurrency Control (MVCC) to handle concurrent data access without locking readers out of writers or writers out of readers. Understanding MVCC internals is crucial for optimizing high-throughput database systems."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Core Concepts: XMIN and XMAX"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Every table row (tuple) in PostgreSQL contains hidden system columns that govern its visibility. The most important fields for concurrency control are xmin and xmax."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"xmin: The transaction ID (txid) of the transaction that inserted the row version."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"xmax: The transaction ID of the transaction that deleted or updated the row version. If the row is active, xmax is 0."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Examining System Columns"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can inspect these hidden metadata columns directly in any PostgreSQL table using the following query:"},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"SELECT xmin, xmax, ctid, * FROM your_table_name;"},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"How Updates Work: INSERT + DELETE"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"Unlike some databases that perform in-place updates with undo logs, PostgreSQL implements an update as an INSERT followed by a DELETE. When a row is updated, the old tuple's xmax is set to the current transaction ID, and a completely new tuple is inserted with its xmin set to the current transaction ID."},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"The Role of VACUUM"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Because updates create dead tuples (rows where xmax is set and no active transaction can see them), tables accumulate bloat. The VACUUM process reclaims storage occupied by dead tuples, making space available for future insertions."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"VACUUM ANALYSE your_table_name;"}]
